teaching.task: # Maths S11 D01: How does a statistical investigation start? An issue, a statistical question for a target population, and a survey with clear language, unambiguous questions and the right number of choices (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Every statistical investigation follows the same steps. It starts with an issue, something worth finding out about. Then you pose a question that data can answer. Then you collect the data, organise and display it, analyse it, and finally draw a conclusion. Here's the issue we'll follow through this whole topic. Teachers notice that Year 11 students seem tired in first period. Australian guidelines advise people aged fourteen to seventeen to get eight to ten hours of sleep a night. So are our Year 11 students getting enough? The survey comes at the collect step, but it can only be as good as the question before it. In every video from here on, the strip shows which step we're on. An issue is too vague to measure. Do students sleep enough? Enough for what, and which students? A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data that varies. How long did I sleep last night has just one answer, so it isn't statistical. How many hours do Year 11 students at our school sleep on a school night expects lots of different answers, and that's what makes it statistical. A good statistical question tells you what to measure, and who to measure it for. Notice this one names who we're asking about. That group is the target population, the whole group you want to know about. Here it's the two hundred Year 11 students at our school, not every teenager in Australia. We'll usually only ask some of them. That part is called the sample, and choosing it fairly is coming soon. Now the survey itself. The first principle is clear language. Use the plain words your target population actually uses. How would you rate your sleep hygiene sounds official, but many students won't know what sleep hygiene means, so their answers will mean different things. People rarely skip a question they don't understand. They guess, and a guess looks just like a real answer. Vague words cause the same problem. Do you often sleep badly? One person's often is twice a week, and another's is every night. Ask for something people can answer exactly. How many hours did you sleep? Every person reads that the same way.

scenes.teachingReason: An issue is too vague to measure. Do students sleep enough? Enough for what, and which students? A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data that varies. How long did I sleep last night has just one answer, so it isn't statistical. How many hours do Year 11 students at our school sleep on a school night expects lots of different answers, and that's what makes it statistical. A good statistical question tells you what to measure, and who to measure it for. Notice this one names who we're asking about. That group is the target population, the whole group you want to know about. Here it's the two hundred Year 11 students at our school, not every teenager in Australia. We'll usually only ask some of them. That part is called the sample, and choosing it fairly is coming soon.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the survey itself. The first principle is clear language. Use the plain words your target population actually uses. How would you rate your sleep hygiene sounds official, but many students won't know what sleep hygiene means, so their answers will mean different things. People rarely skip a question they don't understand. They guess, and a guess looks just like a real answer. Vague words cause the same problem. Do you often sleep badly? One person's often is twice a week, and another's is every night. Ask for something people can answer exactly. How many hours did you sleep? Every person reads that the same way.

scenes.teachingReason: The second principle is that each question has only one possible meaning. Watch for three traps. First, two ideas in one question. How many hours do you sleep and use your phone in bed? Someone who sleeps eight hours and scrolls for one can't answer that, so split it into two questions. Second, a missing time frame. Last night might be a Saturday, when people sleep in, so say on your last school night, Sunday to Thursday, and every answer is about the same kind of night. Third, answer boxes that overlap. Seven to eight and eight to nine both contain eight, so an eight hour sleeper can pick either. Make it seven to under eight, and eight to under nine. Now every eight lands in one place. Each fix removes a second way to read the question.

scenes.teachingReason: The third principle is the number of choices. Too few, and you lose information. Do you get enough sleep, yes or no, can't tell us how much. Too many, and people stop reading. A list of every half hour from nothing to twelve is twenty-five buttons. Somewhere in between works. The choices must also cover every possible answer, so nobody is left out. Over nine leaves out exactly nine, so make the last box nine or more. Now the four boxes fit every answer, each in exactly one place. Another option is a box where people type the number, to the nearest half hour. And if you ask people to rate something, an odd number of choices, like five, gives a fair middle option.
